issue_context.title: Enumerable.Chunk throws OutOfMemoryException for very large chunk sizes.
issue_context.body:
### Description

The exception is thrown even if the actual size of the enumerable is very small and the operation could (in theory) complete.

### Reproduction Steps

```
new[] { 1 }.Chunk(int.MaxValue).ToArray();
```

### Expected behavior

Returns a single element enumerable with a single chunk array of length 1.

### Actual behavior

Throws `OutOfMemoryException` due to attempting to allocate a large array.

### Regression?

_No response_

### Known Workarounds

_No response_

### Configuration

.NET 6, VS2022, Windows 10 x64.

### Other information

One could argue that this shouldn't be fixed because callers just shouldn't ask for chunks that large. However, this can come up when using `int.MaxValue` as a means of "disabling" chunking/batching, especially when said batching is performed deeper in the call stack.

A fix for this would be to special case the creation of the first chunk when size is above a certain threshold. For large sizes, we can assume that the chunk probably won't fill and therefore we can build up to the full size (as is done for `ToArray()` rather than starting by trying to allocate the final array).

> However, this can come up when using int.MaxValue as a means of "disabling" chunking/batching

Technically Chunk can operate on data longer than int.MaxValue, e.g. "infinite" iterator and we don't know input's Length in advance. The best that we can do is to check input IEnumerable whether it's some known type of array/list we can query Length/Count from

> Technically Chunk can operate on data longer than int.MaxValue

True, hence the quotes around disabling. That said there are plenty of scenarios where you know that the upper bound is less than int max (e. g. if the original source was a collection).

> The best that we can do is to check input IEnumerable whether it's some known type of array/list we can query Length/Count from

I agree that there's nothing we can do about the general case of > ArrayMax elements in source with size > ArrayMax. However, if it is *desirable* that Chunk() should succeed in scenarios where there are <= ArrayMax elements with size > ArrayMax that is achievable.

>  That said there are plenty of scenarios where you know that the upper bound is less than int max (e. g. if the original source was a collection).

Want to file a PR with this change? (If BCL folks aren't against this idea)

Is this a real problem one would encounter though? It sounds to me like we'd be making the method slower for everyone simply to make it better behaved in a pathological scenario. Throwing OOM seems like an appropriate behavior (since most likely it's caused by a user bug).

> However, this can come up when using int.MaxValue as a means of "disabling" chunking/batching, especially when said batching is performed deeper in the call stack.

So you're suggesting we special-case `int.MaxValue` as infinity rather than checking if the source count is less than the `size` parameter in the special case? Is there precedent for that in other APIs?

> we'd be making the method slower for everyone simply to make it better behaved in a pathological scenario

I think it's not a pathological scenario, e.g. `new int[] {1,2,3}.Chunk(1000)` where it will allocate an int[1000] while it could just pay a little of perf for casts and allocate only `int[3]`.
You could always use the fancy new ``TryGetNonEnumeratedCount`` to see if you can optimize the chunk before allocating the full size in the fallback.

> I think it's not a pathological scenario, e.g. new int[] {1,2,3}.Chunk(1000) where it will allocate an int[1000] while it could just pay a little of perf for casts and allocate only int[3].

Sure, but it's not pay for play. Now you're forcing every call to invoke `TryGetNonEnumeratedCount` even though this method is mostly used in Rx-style streaming applications where `source` is typically not a collection and `size` is typically a constant parameter.

>  it will allocate an int[1000] while it could just pay a little of perf for casts and allocate only int[3].

FWIW the same issue also applies to sources of length 1003 for the final chunk. That's by design though, it's an explicit trade-off to using `List<T>` for building the intermediate chunks.

> Is this a real problem one would encounter though?

@eiriktsarpalis for context, we've have had this utility method in our internal utility for years and I was looking to replace it with `Chunk()`. Our version handles the "large size" use case because we found that developers expected to be able to "turn off" chunking inline by passing a large value and were surprised that the implementation would actually insist on pre-allocating arrays of the chunk size regardless of how large it was. 

For example, imagine a function like this that uses `Chunk` internally:

```
void CreateRecords(IEnumerable<...> items, ..., int maxBatchSize);
```

Encountering an `OutOfMemoryException` when the application is not actually out of memory is somewhat confusing too (the message does clarify).

> So you're suggesting we special-case int.MaxValue as infinity

I wouldn't propose special-casing int max. I think there is something to be said for the method returning successfully in cases where it can do so. Based on the description of what `Chunk()` does, calling it with `Count()` <= ArrayMax seems like it should always succeed (provided sufficient memory); the fact that it doesn't is due to the specifics of the implementation.

> Is there precedent for that in other APIs?

`Skip()` and `Take()` both work as expected with int max and the code makes a point of supporting this (see https://source.dot.net/#System.Linq/System/Linq/Partition.SpeedOpt.cs,304 and https://source.dot.net/#System.Linq/System/Linq/Partition.SpeedOpt.cs,421). It's not exactly the same thing, just philosophically similar. I'd be willing to bet that 99% of people calling `.Take(int.MaxValue)` are doing it to "take everything" vs. actually working with more than int max elements.

> It sounds to me like we'd be making the method slower ... it's not pay for play

I'm imagining that any special handling would come into play only when `size` is above a certain threshold. Anyone below the threshold wouldn't pay the cost other than the single integer comparison.

If the threshold were ArrayMax, then there is effectively no cost because the method always fails in that case currently.

Possibly there are lower thresholds where the cost of allocating memory upfront when it often won't all be used is worse than the cost of having to grow the array when the memory will be used.

> Want to file a PR with this change? (If BCL folks aren't against this idea)

Sure, provided there is a path forward that all are happy with (doesn't seem like the case currently).

> we found that developers expected to be able to "turn off" chunking inline by passing a large value

FWIW, I don't think this is a reasonable expectation the implementation needs to account for.  If the shape of the method you exposed, the context in which you exposed it, etc. makes it more likely that developers would have such an expectation, your CreateRecords wrapper can simply skip the chunking and just ToArray above whatever threshold makes sense for your application.  Enumerable.Chunk docs are explicit about creating arrays of the specified size; that's not the case with Enumerable.Take.

> Sure, but it's not pay for play. Now you're forcing every call to invoke TryGetNonEnumeratedCount even though this method is mostly used in Rx-style streaming applications where source is typically not a collection and size is typically a constant parameter.

I agree it's not pay-for-play and that pay-for-play is in general the goal, but at the same time, the ship sailed on Enumerable.Chunk being concerned with top performance when we decided that every chunk would be a brand new array allocation.  If we think there's a meaningful number of cases where the input's size can be determined up front and where it'd be smaller than the specified chunk size, adding a fast-path that just handles a single chunk seems ok. (It'd be good to validate the perf impact, though, regardless.)

> will have different observable behaviour 

FWIW, there are tons of things LINQ does dynamically based on the input source that have observable behavior, e.g. using a source's `ICollection<T>` interface rather than its `IEnumerable<T>` interface if it implements that interface.
Sure, but don't these primarily concern performance or perhaps impacting lambdas containing side-effects? This seems like divergence of a different order.

> Sure, but don't these primarily concern performance or perhaps impacting lambdas containing side-effects?

If a source's `IEnumerable<T>` does something functionally different from its `ICollection<T>`, that's a pretty observable difference.  For example, these optimizations are the reason the concurrent collections don't necessarily play well with Enumerable.ToArray: if it were just always enumerating with `IEnumerable<T>`, no problem, but when it checks for `ICollection<T>`, it uses `Count` and `CopyTo`, which could blow up if additional items are added to the collection between the two calls.

> We might want to consider solving the issue in the general case using List<T> to build the chunks

@eiriktsarpalis can't you (to some degree) have your cake and eat it too if you use the existing logic for size < X and the list logic for size > X?

> different observable behaviour depending on whether source is countable or not

FWIW, as a consumer of this API I would prefer that it either consistently works or consistently doesn't in particular scenarios. I see the countable special-case as an implementation option *if* it is decided that avoiding OOM for large chunks is desirable.

I have encountered this, and I've done the "disabling". In my own utility method I make sure to not eagerly allocate large arrays.

Finding out about this issue, I will not be able to replace my utility method. My code would break.

It's not just about OOM. It's undesirable to allocate a 1 million element array if the actual sequence is just a few items. Let's say you batch database inserts 1 million items at a time but it is common to have just a few.

Special-casing `int.MaxValue` is not necessary and not a sufficient fix. There should be an upper bound on the internal array allocation. You could argue for something as low as 4 (optimize for small actual item counts) and as something as high as 64000 (just prevent massive allocations that turn out to be unnecessary).

It's a difficult choice to make but, from my experience, large arguments and small item counts are a very real scenario.
I wouldn't be opposed to a solution that reverts to using a list when `size` exceeds a given threshold. It might help running benchmarks to determine the appropriate cutoff.

> I wouldn't be opposed to a solution that reverts to using a list when size exceeds a given threshold. It might help running benchmarks to determine the appropriate cutoff.

If we're going to do that, I'd prefer we just keep it simple and always do that, regardless of the chunk size specified.

Created https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/67210 to demonstrate the behavior I'm imagining. The idea is to special-case just the first chunk because that's where you run into the large size, small source edge-case.

@stephentoub just saw your post; is your thought about always using lists to keep code-size smaller?

> The idea is to special-case just the first chunk because that's where you run into the large size, small source edge-case.

It's not worth special-casing, nor do we have an ability to pick the right threshold... no matter what we pick, issues like this one will say it's improper. If we're going to change the code to use a list, we should just always use a list and keep it simple.

> It's not worth special-casing

Using a single `List<T>` to buffer each chunk seems reasonable. 

The extra cost of this vs. special-casing the first chunk is just having to clear the list between iterations and having to copy the elements one more time from the list to the array, right?

On my machine, using a list for every chunk is about 10-15% slower than just using a list for the first chunk, which isn't too bad. 

Both approaches are *much* better than the current implementation in lopsided cases like chunk size 1,000,000 with just 10 elements.

Do you think that using a list every time is better than the current implementation given that it supports the lopsided cases better?
I think the real problem here is API design. Wouldn't it be better if `Chunk` returned `IEnumerable<IEnumerable<TSource>>` instead?

> I think the real problem here is API design. Wouldn't it be better if Chunk returned IEnumerable<IEnumerable<TSource>> instead?

This was discussed in the API review:
https://youtu.be/efvl_wtYSw8?t=4377

Effectively sticking with `T[]` was a decision that this is not a super high-performance method.  We thus shouldn't bend over backwards now to try to make it so given the chosen shape.  We can do little tweaks to make it better, but if we're allocating a new large array for every chunk, we've already given up the biggest possible wins.

review_comments: I would recommend presizing the List up to a "reasonable" chunk size (e.g. `new(Math.Min(chunkSize, 128))`) to prevent unneeded resizes when the first chunk is filled. You could use benchmarks to determine a good cutoff number.

This assumes there's going to be enough to fill a chunk. Do we know that's a good assumption? Benchmarks here can be used to show that any size is optimal, so how are you going to choose the benchmarks to use? To me, the reasonable sizes to use are either the chunk size (which the presence of this pr is dismissing) or the small, default value list uses internally so this method is out of the guessing game.
